planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in fall in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; bitterroot needs a dry summer dormancy and rots quickly if watered or left in moist soil after its brief spring growth cycle.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in fall in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; bitterroot needs a dry summer dormancy and rots quickly if watered or left in moist soil after its brief spring growth cycle. Fleshy, needle-like leaves emerge briefly in early spring from a thick, edible taproot, dying back just as large, silky-petaled, pink to white flowers open low to the ground, an ephemeral, dramatic bloom that gave the state flower of Montana its name and made the root a historically important food source for Indigenous peoples of the Northern Rockies and Columbia Plateau, who harvested and dried it before flowering. Native to dry, rocky plains, grasslands, and open pine woods across the intermountain West, it goes fully dormant and disappears entirely above ground for most of the year, making a rock garden or scree bed with excellent drainage the only realistic home for this demanding but spectacular alpine native. Never water during summer dormancy, and mark the planting location clearly since the plant is completely invisible above ground for much of the year.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; northern bluebells thrives in cool, moist woodland conditions and struggles with heat and drought.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; northern bluebells thrives in cool, moist woodland conditions and struggles with heat and drought. Soft, hairy, gray-green leaves support loose, nodding clusters of small, bell-shaped flowers that open pink and mature to true sky blue on the same plant, a color transition typical of the genus, blooming through much of the summer in the cool, moist forests, meadows, and streamside habitats of the northern Rockies and boreal regions where it grows natively. Its tolerance for shade and moist soil, combined with a longer summer bloom period than many spring-ephemeral relatives, makes it a good choice for a cool-climate woodland garden or streamside planting where its native range's summer moisture can be approximated. Keep soil consistently moist through the growing season, and provide afternoon shade in warmer parts of its hardiness range to keep it from stressing in summer heat.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring alongside a compatible host grass or perennial in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Castilleja species are hemiparasitic and establish and flower far better with a suitable host plant's roots nearby.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring alongside a compatible host grass or perennial in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Castilleja species are hemiparasitic and establish and flower far better with a suitable host plant's roots nearby. Brilliant scarlet-red, brush-like flower spikes — actually colorful bracts surrounding small, inconspicuous true flowers — top upright stems from midsummer through fall across mountain meadows and open forests of the western United States and Canada, making it one of the most widely recognized and photographed wildflowers of the Rocky Mountain region and a major hummingbird nectar source. As a hemiparasite it photosynthesizes on its own but also taps into the roots of a neighboring host plant, typically a native grass or aster-family perennial, for water and nutrients, and it rarely thrives or persists long in cultivation without such a host planted nearby. Interplant with a compatible native grass such as blue grama or a native aster, and avoid rich, heavily fertilized soil, which paintbrush species do not tolerate well.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Davidson's penstemon is a high-alpine mat-forming species that needs sharp drainage and struggles with heat and humidity.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Davidson's penstemon is a high-alpine mat-forming species that needs sharp drainage and struggles with heat and humidity. Small, glossy, evergreen leaves form a dense, low, woody mat that hugs rocky ground closely, studded in early summer with large, vivid violet-blue, tubular flowers disproportionately showy for the plant's diminutive scale, native to high-elevation talus slopes and rocky ridges from the Cascades through the Sierra Nevada. Its tight, cushion-forming habit and tolerance of thin, rocky alpine soil make it a choice specimen for a trough garden, rock garden crevice, or alpine bed in a cool-summer climate, but it performs poorly in hot, humid regions far from its high-mountain origins. Water sparingly, provide sharp drainage above all else, and avoid any soil enrichment, which this lean-soil specialist does not need or tolerate.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; shrubby penstemon needs sharp drainage and is drought-tolerant once established, thriving in a rock garden or dry border.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; shrubby penstemon needs sharp drainage and is drought-tolerant once established, thriving in a rock garden or dry border. Small, evergreen, toothed leaves cover a low, woody-based, mounding subshrub that produces an abundant flush of large, vivid lavender-blue to violet flowers in late spring, native to rocky slopes, ridges, and open pine forests across the inland Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies. Its semi-woody, shrubby structure gives it more year-round garden presence than many herbaceous penstemons, holding a tidy mounded shape through winter, and its drought tolerance and rock-garden scale make it well suited to a xeriscape border or scree planting. Cut back lightly after flowering to maintain a compact form, and avoid rich soil or excess summer water, both of which shorten this dryland native's lifespan.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; cliff penstemon is adapted to rocky cliff faces and needs sharp drainage, ideally planted at an angle or in a rock wall crevice.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; cliff penstemon is adapted to rocky cliff faces and needs sharp drainage, ideally planted at an angle or in a rock wall crevice. Small, rounded, blue-gray leaves form a dense, trailing mat that cascades over rock, studded in late spring and early summer with large, vivid magenta-pink flowers disproportionately showy for its low, ground-hugging scale, native to rocky cliffs and outcrops in the Cascade and Siskiyou mountain ranges. Its naturally cliff-dwelling habit makes it an outstanding choice for a rock wall, crevice garden, or steeply sloped scree bed where its trailing stems can drape over an edge, tolerating thin, rocky, nutrient-poor soil that would stress richer garden plants. Water sparingly once established, plant at an angle or on a slope to shed excess moisture from the crown, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; spreading phlox is a high-elevation cushion plant that needs sharp drainage and struggles with heat, humidity, and rich soil.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; spreading phlox is a high-elevation cushion plant that needs sharp drainage and struggles with heat, humidity, and rich soil. Tiny, needle-like evergreen leaves form a dense, low cushion or mat that all but disappears beneath a smothering flush of small, fragrant, pale pink to lavender-blue flowers in late spring, native to dry, rocky, high-elevation slopes and open pine forests from the Cascades and Sierra Nevada into the Rocky Mountains. Its tight, mat-forming habit and tolerance of thin, gravelly, alpine soil make it an excellent choice for a rock garden, scree bed, or trough planting in a cool-summer climate, blanketing bare rocky ground with color for several weeks each spring. Water sparingly, ensure sharp drainage, and avoid rich or heavily amended soil, which causes this lean-soil alpine specialist to decline.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; broadleaf stonecrop tolerates both rocky outcrop conditions and light shade better than many sun-loving sedums.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; broadleaf stonecrop tolerates both rocky outcrop conditions and light shade better than many sun-loving sedums. Flat, powdery, blue-gray to silvery rosettes, often blushed purple-red in bright light, spread into a dense, low mat studded with bright yellow, star-shaped flower clusters in late spring, native to rock outcrops, cliffs, and thin forest soils along the Pacific Coast from California to British Columbia. Its natural tolerance for both sun and partial shade sets it apart from many other native sedums, making it a versatile groundcover for a rock garden, green roof planting, or the thin soil at the base of established trees. Water only occasionally once established, and divide congested mats to propagate or refresh an aging planting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Thunderbird is a more compact, heavier-fruiting selection of evergreen huckleberry bred for improved garden and orchard performance.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Thunderbird is a more compact, heavier-fruiting selection of evergreen huckleberry bred for improved garden and orchard performance. Small, glossy, dark evergreen leaves emerge bronze-red on new growth, covering a naturally more compact, dense shrub than the wild species, which produces small, sweet-tart, dark purple berries in late summer and fall prized for pies, jams, and fresh eating, historically an important traditional food for Pacific Coast Indigenous peoples. Native to coastal forests from British Columbia to California, it thrives in the dappled shade and acidic, humus-rich soil of a woodland understory, and its glossy evergreen foliage is also cut and sold commercially in the florist trade. Mulch with pine needles or acidic compost to maintain soil pH, water regularly during establishment and fruit development, and expect the heaviest fruit set with a bit of morning sun.
